recent_posts.title: Why the three pillars model destroys observability data and why agents need better
recent_posts.summary: The three pillars model of observability (metrics, logs, traces stored in separate silos) destroys the relational context that makes telemetry data valuable. Data power grows combinatorially with each additional attribute, but siloing signals severs those relationships irreparably. AI-SRE agents are already bypassing traditional observability data in favor of richer, pre-digested telemetry with connective tissue intact. As agentic development accelerates change rates dramatically, precise production validation becomes critical — and that requires wide, context-rich, high-cardinality data stored together, not fragmented across pillars. AI-driven joins across silos cannot restore what was destroyed at write time.

recent_posts.title: My (hypothetical) SRECon26 keynote (xpost)
recent_posts.summary: A reflection on how views on generative AI have shifted over the past year, framed as a hypothetical SRECon26 keynote. The author, who co-delivered a cautious 'don't be reflexively antagonistic' message at SRECon25, now fully acknowledges that AI has fundamentally changed software development and the shift is accelerating. The new message for SREs: stop waiting for change to arrive, actively engage with AI tools, know your own cognitive biases, avoid both panic and blind optimism, and lean into outcome-oriented thinking. SREs are well-positioned for this era because they've always been judged by results rather than craft, making them natural builders of AI guardrails and reliability systems.

recent_posts.title: How community feedback forced a complete rewrite of an observability book
recent_posts.summary: Charity Majors shares the story of scrapping and rewriting a major section of her observability book after community feedback revealed she had written tactical advice for engineering teams when the real problem was strategic misalignment at the leadership level. After soliciting input from SREs, CTOs, VPs, and CISOs, she discovered that most observability failures stem from broken buying processes and lack of shared vocabulary between engineering and business stakeholders — not implementation challenges. The rewritten Part 6, 'Observability Governance,' is now structured for technical decision-makers and uses systems thinking language instead of jargon, covering topics from making the business case for observability to vendor partnerships and build-vs-buy decisions. The post also argues that observability is more critical than ever in an AI-native world, since organizational learning speed — enabled by observability — is now the primary constraint on engineering productivity.

recent_posts.title: Writing the second edition of observability engineering
recent_posts.summary: The second edition of "Observability Engineering" is nearly complete and will be almost twice as long as the first edition. The new version has a clearer mission, focusing on software engineers instrumenting code and analyzing production systems with AI. Major updates include comprehensive coverage of OpenTelemetry, AI-era observability practices, and contributions from industry experts. A new section on "Observability Governance" addresses cost containment and tool migrations for platform teams. The book reflects how much the observability landscape has evolved since 2018, when Honeycomb was the only observability company.

recent_posts.title: Operations engineering deserves respect as a critical technical discipline
recent_posts.summary: Operations engineering deserves respect and recognition as a critical technical discipline, not dismissal as toil or lesser work. The distinction between dev and ops is about separation of concerns—building features versus maintaining resilient infrastructure—not coding ability. Operations absorbs the hardest technical problems to make product development simpler. The industry's abandonment of "ops" as a term of pride has created a harmful feedback loop where talented engineers avoid operations roles, leading to poor operational outcomes. Platform engineering is essentially ops with product thinking applied. Clear naming and role definition matter because teams can't optimize for both efficiency (ops) and investment (product) simultaneously.

recent_posts.title: Freeze merges not deploys during holidays
recent_posts.summary: Deploy freezes during holidays or weekends are pragmatic workarounds for teams lacking robust observability, not virtues to celebrate. The better approach is freezing merges instead of deploys to prevent snowballing changes, and continuing to run the deploy process without shipping new code to catch systemic issues that emerge from deployment inactivity. Teams with high-quality observability can maintain deployment velocity while reducing change rate during holiday periods.

recent_posts.title: 2025 was for AI what 2010 was for cloud (xpost)
recent_posts.summary: AI has transitioned from experimental satellite technology to mainstream foundational infrastructure in 2025, mirroring cloud computing's shift around 2010. Drawing from personal experience at Linden Lab during the early AWS days, the author reflects on how experimental cloud projects gradually became the engineering mainstream while datacenters became legacy. Despite ongoing hype cycles and valid skepticism, AI has crossed the threshold from separable technology to core infrastructure, particularly in developer tools. The existence of a bubble doesn't negate fundamental value, just as cloud and internet bubbles didn't invalidate those transformative technologies.

recent_posts.title: Hello World (xpost from substack)
recent_posts.summary: A tech industry figure explains their decision to migrate from WordPress to Substack despite ethical concerns raised by community members. The author justifies the move by emphasizing the need to be more active in technical discussions and reduce friction in content creation. They acknowledge the controversy around Substack's platform policies but conclude this isn't their battle to fight, while implementing mitigations like refusing paid subscriptions and cross-posting to WordPress.

recent_posts.title: Moving from WordPress to Substack
recent_posts.summary: A developer announces their migration from WordPress to Substack after a decade of blogging. The move is motivated by frustration with WordPress and the desire to join the more vibrant tech writing community on Substack. The author is working on the second edition of "Observability Engineering" and plans to share insights from that process. Email subscribers are being migrated, but comments cannot be transferred, and the original site will remain accessible to preserve existing links.

recent_posts.title: From Cloudwashing to O11ywashing
recent_posts.summary: The term 'observability' has been co-opted by vendors to mean traditional monitoring tools that only track system uptime, losing its original meaning of understanding service quality from each customer's perspective. This 'o11ywashing' mirrors the 'cloudwashing' phenomenon where vendors rebrand existing products with trendy terminology. True observability requires unified telemetry combining app, business, and system data to slice by customer ID and other dimensions, not just separate metrics, logs, and traces. Engineering executives need better education on this distinction to avoid investing in rebranded monitoring tools that can't solve their actual problems.

top_posts.title: Why the three pillars of observability are a marketing myth
top_posts.summary: A critical examination of the "three pillars of observability" (metrics, logs, traces) framework, arguing it's primarily a marketing construct that leads to expensive, siloed tooling. The piece advocates for unified storage models (observability 2.0) that treat all telemetry signals as interconnected structured data, eliminating the need to hop between separate systems. It clarifies that OpenTelemetry uses "signals" as the technical term, not "pillars," and explains how modern observability tools can store data once while deriving multiple signal types from the same source, reducing costs and cognitive load.

top_posts.title: On How Long it Takes to Know if a Job is Right for You or Not
top_posts.summary: Trust your gut instincts about new jobs - first impressions within the first week are remarkably accurate predictors of long-term job satisfaction. For managers especially, company alignment is crucial since management work requires representing the organization and its values. Red flags include leadership teams grown entirely from within, creating groupthink. Rather than waiting months to see if things improve, recognize early warning signs and plan accordingly while learning from the experience to avoid similar situations in future roles.

top_posts.title: Why Should You (Or Anyone) Become An Engineering Manager?
top_posts.summary: The article discusses the reasons why someone should consider becoming an engineering manager. It highlights the changing perception of management and the importance of good engineering managers in driving productivity and quality. The article also mentions the skills that can be developed through management, and how it can benefit personal growth and relationships.
